Formerly the ṛṣi Aṅgiras had a son named Nītimañjari [as printed]. In his line the ṛṣi named Sudhanvan had three sons, Ṛbhu, Vibhu and Vāja. There is the custom of calling all three sons of Sudhanvan, Ṛbhu and the rest, Ṛbhus; all three sons are called by the name of the eldest. Since they are pupils of Tvaṣṭṛ, they are also called the craftsmen of the gods. Since they have the very powers and capacities of the deities, the ṛṣis, regarding them as belonging to the group of the deities, have described them and their works in various ways. It is believed that they dwell in the sun's orb and do their works through the sun's rays. **Translation:** "The sūkta *yatra grāvā* is the fifth [of this anuvāka] and has nine riks. The first six are in Anuṣṭubh; the three beginning *āyajī* are in Gāyatrī. Of the first four the deity is Indra; then two have the mortar (*ulūkhala*) as deity; the two that come next have both mortar and pestle (*musala*); of the last, *ucchiṣṭam*, the deity is one of these: Hariścandra, the pressing-skin (*adhiṣavaṇa-carma*) or Soma. So the Bṛhaddevatā says: 'with the last [rik] he praises either the pressing-skin or the Soma' (Bṛ. 3-411 as printed). So also the Anukramaṇikā: '*yatra grāvā*, nine, six Anuṣṭubh at the beginning; *yac cid dhi*, two to the mortar; the next two to the pestle as well; the last, of Prajāpati Hariścandra, is in praise of the skin.' The first four are applied in the *homa* at the *añjaḥsava*; the four from the fifth in the pressing; the last at the *Droṇakalaśa*, in the pouring-down of the Soma. So the Brāhmaṇa: 'Then Śunaḥśepa saw this *añjaḥsava*; he pressed it with these four; with *yac cid dhi tvaṃ gṛhe gṛhe* he then poured it down into the *Droṇakalaśa*; with the rik *ucchiṣṭaṃ camvor bhara*; then, when [Hariścandra] had taken hold of him, he offered it with the four former [riks] with the *svāhā*-call' (Ai. **॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥** *(pp. 430–431)* **आयजी** — *sarvato yajñasādhane*: the two implements of sacrifice on every side, i.e. the mortar and the pestle; this is a dual form. **वाजसातमा** — *vājaṃ sanotīti vājasāḥ*; *atiśayena vājasāḥ vājasātamau*: *vāja* means food; by giving it the mortar and the pestle are called *vājasātamā*; by pounding grain in the mortar with the help of the pestle one prepares food; so they are said to give the food and the like. **उच्चा** — *uccaiḥ*, with a loud sound: when grain is pounded with the pestle in the mortar, a loud sound is natural. **विजर्भृतः** — *hṛñ haraṇe*: they sport; they seem to sport. **हरी इव** — like Indra's horses; the two horses of Indra are called *harī*; Yāska gives the derivation *harī indrasya* ('the two bay horses of Indra'). **अन्धांसि** — foods: *andhaḥ* (Ni. 5-1, as printed) is a name for food. **बप्सता** — *bhasa bhakṣaṇadīptyoḥ*: eating, chewing; **Translation:** "Impelled by the Viśvedevas, Śunaḥśepa praised Indra with the twenty-two riks beginning with this one. So the Brāhmaṇa says: 'The Viśvedevas said to him: "Indra is the most vigorous, the strongest, the mightiest, the best, the most capable of carrying across of the gods; praise him now; then we shall release you."
